From what I can see, speech recognition is the hot subfield of acoustics, because it has hitched itself to artificial intelligence. Combining AI with other areas of acoustics (or with any discipline, really) is also very popular: fault detection and prediction, extracting emotion from recordings to give early warning of violent incidents, audio classification and so on.

NVH has been developing steadily in China in recent years, and more and more carmakers are investing in it. A while ago I joined an NVH group chat and was amazed at how many people work in it. With the traditional car industry declining and electric vehicles on the rise, it’s hard to say how the industry as a whole will fare, but nobody has much experience with EV NVH yet. Noise levels have dropped a lot, but switching from combustion engines to electric motors brings plenty of new acoustic problems, so the prospects there are fairly good.

Virtual acoustics had its moment a few years ago, riding the VR hype. Industry has cooled on it in recent years, but in academia it’s still in full swing. Virtual acoustics and auralization touch every corner of acoustics: physical modeling or measurement of complex sources; numerical and geometrical acoustics models of outdoor and indoor sound propagation; 3D reproduction, binaural technology with HRTFs, and Ambisonics; algorithm optimization and hardware such as GPUs and FPGAs to speed up real-time auralization; and, for subjective evaluation, listening tests, psychoacoustic calculations and statistics. It covers a large part of the field.

Which area makes it easiest to publish lots of papers? Speech plus AI, obviously!

Fanyu Meng · 108 consultations · rated 5.0 · Zhihu outstanding answerer in acoustics · PhD in acoustics, RWTH Aachen University
